lead: This morning is the last of Advent. David wants to build God a house, and God answers that he will build David a house instead. In the Gospel an old priest, his voice just restored, sings that the promise has come: God “has raised up a mighty savior for us in the house of his servant David”. A thousand years of waiting end in one sentence, and at evening the Church begins Christmas.

r.h: The Lord will make you a house
set: David has taken Jerusalem and brought the ark there (2 Samuel 5–6). The wars are quiet and he lives in a cedar palace. It seems only right that God should have a house too, and the prophet Nathan at first agrees. This chapter, the oracle of Nathan, is one of the foundations of Israel's hope for the Messiah. It is echoed in Psalm 89, today's psalm.
str: vv. 1–3: David's plan; Nathan's first yes.
vv. 4–5: that night God speaks: “Are you the one?”
vv. 8b–9: I took you from the sheep; I have been with you.
vv. 10–11: a place for Israel, rest, and the promise of a house.
v. 12: your offspring and his kingdom.
vv. 14a, 16: father and son; a house and a throne forever.
kw: The whole oracle turns on this word. It means a building (a palace, a temple) and also a family line. David offers a building; God promises a dynasty.
Literally seed. In the first place it is Solomon, who will build the Temple (7:13; 1 Kings 6). But “forever” goes beyond any one son.
The word comes back in vv. 13 and 16. The kings of David's line fell and the throne stood empty after the exile, but Israel did not stop hoping.
vv: See now, I am living in a house of cedar, but the ark of God stays in a tent.
A generous thought. Yet the story shows that even a good plan for God can be our plan and not his.
Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
God is not refusing honour. He is reversing the direction: grace always begins from God's side.
Moreover the Lord declares to you that the Lord will make you a house.
This is the turning point of the chapter. The man who wanted to give receives.
Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me; your throne shall be established forever.
A note on the text: the standard Hebrew text has “before you”; NRSV and POC read “before me”, with the Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts.
ch: The New Testament reads this oracle of Jesus. Gabriel promises Mary that God will give her son “the throne of his ancestor David”, and “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33), words the Creed repeats. Hebrews 1:5, heard at tomorrow's Mass, applies 7:14 to the Son. The Catechism presents Jesus as the messianic Son of David (CCC 439) and notes that the Temple David wished to build was the work of his son (CCC 2580).

r.h: The dawn from on high will break upon us
set: Zechariah's mouth has just been opened (1:64). Filled with the Holy Spirit, he speaks the song the Church calls the Benedictus, from its first word in Latin. Like the Magnificat, it is made of Old Testament language. It has the form of a Jewish blessing of God for his saving acts. A priest of the old covenant here stands at the door of the new.
str: vv. 67–75: God blessed for what he has done: the savior from David's house, the mercy to the ancestors, the oath to Abraham, so that we may serve him without fear.
vv. 76–77: to the child: you will go before the Lord.
vv. 78–79: the dawn from on high, light in darkness, the way of peace.
kw: Used at the opening (1:68) and the close (1:78). In the Old Testament God “visits” his people to save them (Exodus 4:31).

The word for the rising of the sun or a star. The Greek Old Testament also uses it for the messianic “Branch” (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8). Latin renders it Oriens, the title in the antiphon of 21 December. Compare Malachi 4:2, “the sun of righteousness shall rise”.
The name means “the Lord remembers”. In v. 72 the song says that God “has remembered his holy covenant”.
vv: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favorably on his people and redeemed them.
Jesus has not been born yet, but Zechariah speaks in the past tense. For faith, God's promise is as sure as what has been done.
And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways,
An eight-day-old infant receives his life's task. “The Most High” is the title given to Jesus' Father in 1:32; in Luke “the Lord” also points to Jesus (1:43).
By the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will break upon us,

A note on the text: the manuscripts vary between “will break” (which NRSV and POC follow) and “has broken”. Literally “tender mercy” is the “bowels of mercy”, the deep feeling of God. The whole salvation comes out of this.
ch: The Church sings the Benedictus each morning at Morning Prayer, so each day begins with the promise that the dawn is coming. The Catechism calls John “Prophet of the Most High”, the last of the prophets, who goes before Jesus (CCC 523), and says that in him the Holy Spirit concludes his speaking through the prophets (CCC 719).

qa: If God promised a throne forever, what happened when David's line stopped ruling?

The Church's answer is that the promise was greater than a political kingdom. Jesus reigns as the risen Son of David, and his kingdom has no end (Luke 1:33; CCC 439). The Jewish people's long hope for God's anointed is honoured by the Church as part of the same story (CCC 839–840).
rite: This Mass is the last of Advent, in violet, with its own readings. From the evening the Mass of the Vigil of Christmas begins, with the Gospel of the genealogy of Jesus. The title Oriens and the song of Zechariah join here: the dawn this song awaits comes with Christmas.
study: David wanted to build for God, and God wanted to build for David. Where is my plan for God standing in the way of God's plan for me?
“To guide our feet into the way of peace”: where is my family or parish most in need of that way this Christmas?
